tagline: The 15th-century tower where chemist Charles Macintosh reportedly perfected his waterproof fabric now anchors a £10 million restoration and Scotland's newest 5-star castle-hotel
highlights: Land acquired by Alexander Lindsay in 1440; the original defensive tower dates to the 15th century
Once owned by 19th-century chemist Charles Macintosh, who patented his famous waterproof fabric — the origin of the word 'mackintosh' — during his time as owner of Crossbasket
Listed on Scotland's 'Buildings at Risk' register before its restoration
Bought in 2011 by Alison and Steve Timoney, who invested over £10 million across a 5-year restoration reviving the 15th-century tower and reinstating period craftsmanship
Reopened in May 2016 as a 5-star hotel with 49 rooms in total: 9 historic castle rooms, each named after a different historic custodian, plus 40 Art Deco-inspired rooms and suites in the new wing
description:
Crossbasket Castle sits on the edge of High Blantyre, a short distance south of Glasgow, and its origins reach back to 1440, when the land was acquired by Alexander Lindsay and a defensive tower house was raised on the site — one of the many small fortified towers that once dotted the Clyde valley to protect landholders and their tenants. The castle's most quietly remarkable historical association, however, belongs to the 19th century, when Crossbasket was owned by the chemist Charles Macintosh. It was during his time as owner of the castle that Macintosh is understood to have developed and patented his famous waterproofed fabric — the invention that gave the English language the word 'mackintosh,' still used today for a rubberised raincoat. Few Scottish castles can claim a direct connection to a piece of everyday vocabulary used across the English-speaking world, and it gives Crossbasket a genuinely distinctive footnote in industrial as well as architectural history.

Like many smaller Scottish tower houses, Crossbasket eventually fell into decline, and by the early 21st century the castle was listed on Scotland's 'Buildings at Risk' register — the official inventory of historic structures in danger of being lost to neglect. Its rescue came in 2011, when Alison and Steve Timoney purchased the castle and committed to what became a five-year, more than £10 million restoration. The project revived the fabric of the original 15th-century tower, reinstating period craftsmanship and detail throughout, while also adding an entirely new wing built in an Art Deco idiom rather than attempting to disguise the addition as historic pastiche — a design choice that gives Crossbasket a genuinely unusual architectural identity, pairing a defensive medieval tower with confident 1920s-inspired glamour under one roof.

The restoration was completed and the castle reopened in May 2016 as a 5-star hotel and events venue. Accommodation today totals 49 rooms across the two distinct wings: nine individually designed rooms and suites within the historic castle itself, each named after a different historic custodian connected to the estate's story — among them the Lindsay Tower Suite, spread across four storeys of the original 15th-century tower with sweeping views over the estate — and forty Art Deco-inspired rooms and suites, including two suites and four junior suites, arranged across two storeys of the new wing.

Crossbasket's daily Afternoon Tea, served from 2pm to 5pm, has built a strong reputation confirmed by non-resident reviews on TripAdvisor and elsewhere, making it accessible to day visitors as well as overnight guests. One practical detail worth knowing before booking: on dates when the historic castle is reserved for exclusive private events, Afternoon Tea service moves to the Art Deco wing rather than the original castle rooms, so visitors hoping specifically for the historic setting should check availability in advance rather than assume it by default.

Just a short drive from Glasgow, Crossbasket offers a genuinely unusual pairing of authentic medieval fabric, a distinctive piece of industrial history, and a fully modern luxury hotel experience — a combination that has quickly established it as one of the more talked-about new castle-hotel openings in Scotland.

The castle also operates as a wedding and events venue, and its grounds along the Rotten Calder river, complete with a landscaped waterfall, have become a popular backdrop for both ceremonies and photography, adding another dimension to a property that already spans nearly six centuries of use — from a defensive Clydeside tower, through Georgian industrial chemistry, to a 21st-century luxury hospitality reinvention.
history: The land at Crossbasket was acquired by Alexander Lindsay in 1440, and a defensive tower house was built on the site in the 15th century. In the 19th century the castle was owned by the chemist Charles Macintosh, who is understood to have developed and patented his famous waterproofed fabric — the origin of the word 'mackintosh' — during his time as owner. The castle later fell into disrepair and was listed on Scotland's 'Buildings at Risk' register before being purchased in 2011 by Alison and Steve Timoney, who carried out a five-year restoration costing more than £10 million, reviving the 15th-century tower and reinstating period craftsmanship while adding an entirely new Art Deco-inspired wing. Crossbasket reopened in May 2016 as a 5-star hotel and events venue with 49 rooms in total.

faqs.question: Can I have Afternoon Tea at Crossbasket Castle without staying overnight?
faqs.answer: Yes. Crossbasket Castle serves Afternoon Tea daily from 2pm to 5pm, and non-resident bookings are confirmed by guest reviews on TripAdvisor and elsewhere. One detail to note: on dates when the historic castle is booked exclusively for private events, Afternoon Tea moves to the Art Deco wing rather than the original castle rooms, so it's worth checking availability in advance if the historic setting specifically is the draw.

faqs.question: Is it true that the word 'mackintosh' comes from Crossbasket Castle?
faqs.answer: The connection is real, though it concerns the owner rather than the building's name directly: the 19th-century chemist Charles Macintosh, who owned Crossbasket Castle, is understood to have developed and patented his famous waterproofed fabric during his time there. That fabric, and the raincoats made from it, gave rise to the word 'mackintosh,' still used today across the English-speaking world.

faqs.question: How many rooms does Crossbasket Castle have?
faqs.answer: Crossbasket Castle has 49 rooms in total: 9 individually designed rooms and suites within the historic 15th-century castle, each named after a different historic custodian of the estate, and 40 Art Deco-inspired rooms and suites — including two suites and four junior suites — in the newly built wing added during the 2011–2016 restoration.
